analysis.one_liner: Closes corporate offshore tax loopholes and tax shelters while trimming the top corporate rate to 34%.
analysis.headline: Senator Kerry's bill to curb offshore tax deferral and tax shelters was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2007 and died there with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make US shareholders pay current tax on most income earned by their foreign subsidiaries instead of letting the tax wait until profits come home. It would treat foreign corporations that are run from the United States as domestic for tax purposes, write the 'economic substance' rule into law so tax shelters with no real business purpose can be penalized 40%, and cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 34%. It was introduced the first week of the 110th Congress and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and domestic businesses that don't use offshore subsidiaries or tax shelters would gain from a broader, more level tax base; the Treasury would collect tax on income that currently sits overseas tax-deferred. Workers at companies that shift profits or jobs offshore are the people the bill's title points to. Corporations with taxable income above the top bracket would also get a small rate cut.

how_it_helps.text: Limits tax deferral by rewriting the rules on controlled foreign corporations, so US shareholders owe current tax on most income earned by their overseas subsidiaries rather than deferring it until the profits are brought home [S2][S3].

Treats publicly traded foreign corporations whose executive officers and senior management are primarily located in the United States as domestic corporations for income tax purposes, closing a way of being American-run but foreign for tax purposes [S3].

Writes the economic substance doctrine into the tax code and imposes a 40% penalty (20% if disclosed on the return) on underpayments from transactions lacking real business purpose, and denies a deduction for interest on those underpayments [S2][S3].
Eliminates the 35% top corporate marginal rate, lowering it to 34% for income above the bracket threshold and for personal service corporations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational companies with foreign subsidiaries would pay more current tax; tax shelter promoters and their advisers would lose a business line; corporations with income in the top bracket would see the rate cut but would face the offshore crackdown alongside it.

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts the top corporate marginal rate from 35% to 34%, reducing what the largest corporations and personal service corporations owe on income above the bracket threshold — a concession to the same companies the offshore provisions target [S3].
It grandfathers foreign earnings accumulated before 2008 and gives companies organized in treaty countries a transition period, so some existing offshore profits avoid the new rules [S3].

The codified economic substance rules and the 40% penalty would apply to any transaction a court finds lacks economic substance, which could raise costs and uncertainty for some legitimate business arrangements, not only abusive shelters [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's center of gravity is cracking down on offshore deferral and shelters, with the one-point rate cut as the offset for business. For ordinary taxpayers the trade is probably favorable: the avoidance crackdown reaches far more money than the small rate cut gives back. The honest weaknesses are the grandfathering of pre-2008 offshore earnings and the risk that the harsh penalty reaches some legitimate transactions.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never acted on it, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Kerry introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, the opening day of the 110th Congress, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history for the entire two-year Congress [S5].

The bill would have limited offshore tax deferral, treated US-managed foreign corporations as domestic, codified the economic substance doctrine with a 40% penalty, and eliminated the 35% top corporate rate [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational companies with foreign subsidiaries and the tax shelter industry, which kept the existing rules for two more years — including the ability to defer US tax on foreign profits and to sell transactions with no purpose beyond tax savings. Ordinary taxpayers gained nothing; the crackdown never happened in this form.

for.name: Sen. John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 110th Congress and delivered introductory remarks on it; no senator joined as a cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 4, 2007 and took no recorded action on it for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Chaired the Finance Committee during the 110th Congress, which never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split is on the record; the bill's only recorded support was a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill taxes most income of controlled foreign corporations currently instead of allowing deferral, and taxes US-managed foreign corporations as domestic. These companies currently defer US tax on foreign profits, a cost that shows up as either higher taxes on everyone else or more borrowing.

industries.industry: Tax shelter promoters and their advisers (accounting and tax law practices)
industries.note: Codifying the economic substance doctrine and attaching a 40% penalty to shelter underpayments directly shrinks the market for transactions whose value comes from tax savings alone. Their revenue comes from arrangements that shift tax onto other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Largest corporations and personal service corporations
industries.note: The bill cuts their top marginal rate from 35% to 34%, a modest gain, but the same companies typically own foreign subsidiaries that would face the new current-tax rules. The net effect depends on how much of their income sits offshore.
